one_liner: Thread-per-core Rust async runtime on io_uring (epoll/kqueue fallback); ~1.9x Tokio's peak echo QPS on 4 cores.
what_it_does: Monoio is a Rust async runtime for network servers, used in place of Tokio. Each thread runs its own single-threaded executor and io_uring ring, and tasks never migrate, so futures and I/O objects need not be Send/Sync. Its I/O traits (AsyncReadRent/AsyncWriteRent) take ownership of the buffer and return it with the result (`(res, buf) = stream.read(buf).await`) instead of borrowing `&mut [u8]` as Tokio's poll-style traits do, so it is not a drop-in replacement. It ships TCP/UDP/Unix sockets, file ops, timers, select!/join! and a #[monoio::main] macro that can start one runtime per worker thread.
how_it_is_fast: It uses completion-based I/O through io_uring. Reads and writes are pushed as SQEs and only submitted when the thread runs out of ready tasks, in one io_uring_enter call (submit_and_wait). Tokio's reactor instead does an epoll_wait and then one read/write syscall per ready socket. The thread-per-core scheduler keeps its state in thread-local Rc/UnsafeCell plus a local VecDeque task queue with no work stealing, so the hot path has no atomics or cross-thread locks. TcpListener sets SO_REUSEPORT by default, so each core accepts its own connections. Because the I/O API takes buffer ownership, the kernel can write straight into user buffers; the project's comparison doc says Glommio copies data at this point for compatibility.
when_to_use: Linux 5.6+ servers with many concurrent connections per core, such as L4/L7 proxies, gateways and RPC front ends, where peak QPS or CPU per request matters. In the maintainers' echo test the lead over Tokio grows with core count: ~1.15x at 1 core, ~1.9x at 4 and ~3x at 16.
Work that shards evenly across cores (NGINX-style), where per-connection state never needs to leave its thread and you want Rc/RefCell instead of Arc/Mutex.
Fixed-load services where CPU headroom matters. At 384k QPS on 4 cores with 250 connections per core, Monoio used ~232% CPU against Tokio's ~390%.

Teams that develop on macOS or older kernels and deploy on io_uring Linux. The default FusionDriver probes io_uring opcode support at startup and otherwise falls back to epoll/kqueue with the same code (MONOIO_FORCE_LEGACY_DRIVER=1 forces the fallback).
when_not_to_use: Unbalanced or bursty per-connection load. There is no work stealing, and the README warns this can make it slower than Tokio because cores sit idle.

Low concurrency on a single core. In the project's own data Tokio had higher QPS up to 480 connections on 1 core (for example 166,938 vs 160,157 at 400 connections) and lower latency at 80 connections per core under fixed load, because io_uring submission latency is higher than epoll's.

Code built mainly on the Tokio ecosystem (tokio::spawn, tokio::sync, reqwest, tonic). Those crates need the poll-io feature (epoll readiness layered over io_uring) or monoio-compat (an extra buffer copy), and both give up most of the io_uring gain on those paths.
Windows, musl or Android targets. Windows is experimental (open issues #274, #403), 0.2.4 fails to compile for musl (#349), and there is an open Android build failure (#324).
Mixed CPU-heavy or blocking work. spawn_blocking needs the `sync` feature and by default runs on the calling thread (BlockingStrategy::ExecuteLocal), which stalls that core's I/O loop.

integration.dependencies: io-uring 0.6 (Linux), mio 0.8 (legacy epoll/kqueue driver), libc, socket2, bytes, pin-project-lite, rustc-hash, memchr, auto-const-array; optional: tokio (poll-io / tokio-compat), flume + threadpool + once_cell (sync), nix (utils: CPU pinning), tracing (debug), ctrlc (signal)
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.75 per the README; Cargo.toml sets no rust-version, and CI runs both stable and nightly. The opt-in `unstable` feature needs nightly. The io_uring driver needs Linux 5.6+; splice needs 5.7+, unlinkat/renameat 5.11+, mkdirat/symlinkat 5.15+. Wait-with-timeout uses ext_arg on 5.11+ and a TimeoutOp fallback otherwise.
integration.platforms: Linux (io_uring or epoll) and macOS (kqueue). CI builds x86_64, aarch64, armv7, riscv64, s390x and loongarch64 Linux plus x86_64/aarch64 macOS. Windows support is experimental.
integration.thread_safety: Thread-per-core: the runtime, tasks and I/O objects stay on the thread that created them, and spawn does not require Send. Cross-thread wakers and channels need the `sync` feature, which adds an eventfd and a waker channel. To scale, start one runtime per thread, either with the worker_threads macro option or with your own threads plus utils::bind_to_cpu_set.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it replaces Tokio as the runtime but has its own I/O API (buffer-ownership AsyncReadRent/AsyncWriteRent, monoio::spawn without a Send bound). Tokio's AsyncRead/AsyncWrite are available three ways: through `poll-io` (TcpStreamPoll, epoll over io_uring), through monoio-compat (extra copy, and you must call flush/shutdown explicitly), or with the legacy-only driver via `tokio-compat` at no overhead.

gotchas: io_uring needs locked memory. With the common 64 KiB memlock default, reads and writes can fail with os error 105 'No buffer space available'. Raise memlock to at least 512 or unlimited. Ring entries default to 1024 (minimum 256); the in-flight op slab starts at 10x entries.

Dropping an in-flight I/O future does not reliably cancel it. The async-cancel feature queues a CancelOp, but the read may still complete and its data is then lost, for example in select!{read, timeout}. Keep the future alive, or use cancelable_read with a Canceller and check for ECANCELED (125).
A panic inside a spawned task kills the runtime thread; unlike Tokio it is not caught (issue #314). Timer APIs panic unless enable_timer() or timer_enabled = true is set.

TcpListener::bind turns on SO_REUSEPORT and SO_REUSEADDR by default, so a second process can quietly share the port; use bind_with_config to disable this. The `zero-copy` feature (MSG_ZEROCOPY) is documented as unstable and possibly slower.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Monoio for a general-purpose Rust network server that wants io_uring throughput from a full runtime (sockets, files, timers, and hyper/h2 via poll-io); PhotonLibOS is the nearest C++ equivalent. aquatic's own io_uring-vs-mio/epoll comparison shows only ~1.11x, so remember that Monoio's 2-3x multi-core lead over Tokio mixes io_uring with thread-per-core scheduling.
verified_claims_summary: This is the maintainers' 2021 ping-pong echo benchmark: rust nightly-2021-11-26 release build with LTO, Linux 5.15.4, a Xeon Gold 5118 server with an X710 10GbE NIC, and the client on a separate machine. With 1 KiB messages on 4 server cores, Monoio peaked at 810,075 QPS against 434,565 for Tokio's multi-thread epoll runtime (1.86x) and 603,016 for Glommio. With 100 B messages on 16 cores it reached 2,802,033 against 917,419. Tokio ran as one unpinned work-stealing runtime with a single accept loop, while Monoio ran one pinned io_uring runtime per core with its own SO_REUSEPORT listener, so the numbers compare runtime architecture plus io_uring rather than io_uring against raw epoll; at 1 core the lead is ~1.15x.
status_note: Active but slow to ship: the repo is now github.com/monoio-rs/monoio (moved from bytedance/monoio) with commits through 2026-05-29, but the last crates.io release is still 0.2.4 from August 2024 (~1.58M downloads), so fixes made since then are only on git master, and open issue #398 asks whether the project is still maintained. It is MIT OR Apache-2.0 and usable as a crate today.
